tuzaklar.dogru: The four original stages are forming, storming, norming and performing; adjourning was added in 1977.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Any collection of people who come together is a team.
tuzaklar.dogru: A group is a sum of individuals; a team is a cohesive coalition working for a shared agenda.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Diverse teams make better decisions because they agree faster.
tuzaklar.dogru: Diverse teams make better decisions because they focus on facts, re-examine them and avoid groupthink.

ozet: A group is a sum of individuals; a team is a cohesive coalition with a shared agenda.
Forming: polite introductions; the team looks to the leader for direction.
Storming: competing for control, conflict, taking sides, frustration about roles.
Norming: ground rules, shared responsibility and respect.
Performing: a self-directed, confident team that gets results.
Adjourning was added in 1977: the team breaks up at the end of the project.
The stages are not linear; a new member or a new task sends the team back.
Diverse teams focus on facts, avoid groupthink and are more innovative.
McKinsey: 35 percent more likely to beat industry returns for ethnic diversity, 15 percent for gender diversity.
lessons.aklinda: Forming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning: meet, clash, set rules, deliver, break up. If a new member joins, go back to storming.
lessons.sinavda: Part 2 tells the short story of a team and asks which stage it is in, or which stages it goes through after a change. It carries about 3 points. The chain of storming after new members join, followed by norming, is the pattern asked most often.

lessons.ad: Social networks: ties, three principles and Ibarra’s network types
lessons.neden: The organization chart shows who reports to whom, but information and help often flow along other paths. Social network concepts give names to these invisible paths. Part 2 describes a relationship that someone builds and asks which type of tie, which principle or which Ibarra network it is.
hedefler: Explain what a social network is and the three advantages it gives leaders.
Tell apart strong ties, weak ties and a bridging tie.
Recognize the principles of reciprocity, exchange and similarity from an example.
Separate Ibarra’s operational, personal and strategic networks in a scenario.

adimlar.anlatim:
When a problem comes up in a company, who does everyone go to? Often not the manager on the chart, but someone who “knows the job”. This behaviour shows that a social network exists.

A Social network is a patterned set of relationships between two or more people (actors). These relationships are drawn in a sociogram: people become dots and relationships become lines. The course notes call networks “the invisible organization”, because they show how communication and resources really flow. The chart shows the official path; the network shows the actual one.

Networks give leaders three advantages:

  • Access to information and knowledge: you can learn what the people you know already know.
  • Access to diverse skill sets: someone you know brings a skill you do not have.
  • Power: a person who connects many people can influence the direction of things.

Do not confuse a social network with the networked team structure in chapter 8: that is a formal type of structure, while a social network is the web of relationships that exists inside any structure.
adimlar.ornek: At an imaginary print shop, the chart says all fault reports go to the production manager. But the new manager Kerem notices that employees first ask Hüsnü, a technician with twenty years in the shop. On the chart Hüsnü is an ordinary technician, but he sits at the centre of the network where knowledge flows. The invisible organization works differently from the chart.

soru.q: A new manager sees that the official chart routes all requests through her, yet staff actually ask a long-serving technician for help first. What does the technician's role reveal?
o: The informal network through which resources really flow
A formal matrix reporting line that gives staff two bosses
A counterculture whose values oppose the firm's main culture
A weak tie in which no resources are exchanged at all
soru.x: Staff use the technician instead of the official path, and this shows the social network where information and help really flow, that is, the invisible organization. The matrix option looks tempting because staff turn to two different people, but matrix is a formal reporting line; here the technician is not a formal boss.

adimlar.anlatim:
The lines in a network are called ties. A tie can be direct (a single connection) or indirect (through other people). Ties also differ in strength.

Strong ties: actors who know each other well and exchange often. Your close friends, and the teammates you work with every day.

Weak ties: actors who know each other at least by name or reputation but have no regular exchange. An old classmate, or a colleague you met once.

The first thing that comes to mind is that strong ties are more useful. But Granovetter showed that people mostly find jobs through weak ties. You can work out why yourself: your close friends move in the same circle as you, so they know what you know. A distant contact moves in another circle and hears about an opportunity you never heard of. So a weak tie carries new information.

To tell them apart, look at two things: how well they know each other and how often they exchange. If both are high, it is strong; if they know each other but exchange rarely, it is weak.
adimlar.ornek: Deniz, an imaginary student, is looking for an internship. The close friends she talks to every day know the same adverts and cannot tell her anything new: strong ties. An old high school friend she runs into once a year mentions an internship at the agency where she works that has not been advertised yet: weak tie. This is exactly Granovetter’s finding.

soru.q: Deniz hears about a job opening from a former classmate she meets perhaps once a year, not from the close friends she sees daily. Which idea best explains this?
o: Weak ties more often bring new, non-overlapping information
Strong ties more often bring new, non-overlapping information
Indirect ties carry no information about job opportunities
Close friends usually hide job openings from each other
soru.x: According to Granovetter, people mostly find jobs through weak ties, because distant contacts bring new information from other circles. The strong ties option looks tempting because close friends are more willing to help, but they already know what you know.

adimlar.anlatim:
Some ties play a special role in a network. A Bridging tie is a tie that provides non-redundant information and resources. “Non-redundant” means this: you cannot get this information any other way. A bridging tie usually links two groups that are cut off from each other; information in one group reaches the other only through that tie. This is why a person in a bridging position is valuable: both sides need them.

Two more concepts describe the overall picture of a network. Centrality is how central an actor is in the network: the more people are connected to them, or the more information passes through them, the more central they are. Density is how many of the people in the network are connected to each other. In a dense network everyone knows everyone.

Do not confuse a bridging tie with a weak tie. Weak tie describes the strength of a tie (how well people know each other, how often they exchange). Bridging tie describes the function of a tie (does it carry information you cannot get elsewhere). If a question says “information neither group gets elsewhere”, the answer is bridging tie.
adimlar.ornek: At an imaginary hospital, the nurse Mert is the only person who talks regularly with both the IT team and the operating theatre team. He carries IT’s plan for the new system to the operating theatre, and the operating theatre’s complaints to IT. Mert’s ties are bridging ties, because the two groups cannot get this information any other way. This also raises Mert’s centrality.

soru.q: At a museum, Selim is the only person who talks regularly with both the curators and the marketing team, and he passes on information that neither group can get anywhere else. His link is best described as a:
soru.x: Selim links two groups and carries information they cannot get any other way, that is, non-redundant information: bridging tie. Strong tie looks tempting because he talks to them regularly, but the question stresses the unique information the tie carries, not its strength.

adimlar.baslik: The principles of reciprocity and exchange
adimlar.anlatim:
Networks do not grow at random. Kilduff and Tsai describe the principles by which ties form in three points. You will see the first two in this step and the third in the next.

Principle of reciprocity: trading favours of roughly equal value. “You helped me with the report, so let me help you with the presentation.” The logic is a sense of fairness: you give back what you received, and so the relationship lasts.

Principle of exchange: trading favours with people who are different from you. Here the gain comes from difference: complementary resources create more value. What a programmer can get from another programmer is limited, but what they get from a marketer is something they do not have at all.

To separate the two, look at this: Is the stress on paying a favour back at equal value, or on the two sides bringing different skills that complete each other? Equal return is reciprocity; complementary difference is exchange. Both principles involve a trade; the difference is where the value comes from.
adimlar.ornek: In an imaginary apartment building, two neighbours take turns every week picking up each other’s child from school: favours of equal value, that is, reciprocity. In the same building, Ayten, who can bake cakes but does not know the internet, makes a deal with a young neighbour who understands social media: she bakes the cakes, and the neighbour runs the sales online. Skills that complete each other: exchange.

soru.q: A café owner who is excellent at baking teams up with a neighbour who runs social media campaigns, because each has a skill the other lacks. Which networking principle is at work?
soru.x: The two sides bring skills that are different and complete each other: this is the exchange principle. Reciprocity looks tempting because it is also a trade of favours, but in reciprocity the stress is on giving back equal value, not on combining different skills.

adimlar.baslik: The similarity principle and the echo chamber
adimlar.anlatim:
The third principle is the most natural one. Principle of similarity: ties form by themselves between people who share a background, values and interests. Graduates of the same school, fans of the same team and people with the same hobby find each other easily. The reason is simple: talking to someone similar is easy, a common language is ready, and trust grows faster.

But this principle carries a risk: the echo chamber. If everyone is alike, everyone thinks the same things and knows the same information. No new ideas come in, and everything that is said echoes back. Link this risk to the earlier steps: similar people mostly share the same information; information you cannot get elsewhere comes from ties that reach into different circles, for example through bridging ties. This is also very close to the idea of groupthink in c10a.

Similarity and exchange are easy to separate, because they are opposites. Similarity comes from likeness and brings comfort; exchange comes from difference and brings complementary value.
adimlar.ornek: The founder of an imaginary start-up builds her team only from friends who graduated from the same department and have the same hobbies. The first months are very comfortable, and everyone agrees at once: similarity. A year later all the ideas look alike, and nobody voices a customer’s different point of view: echo chamber.

soru.q: A start-up founder hires only friends from her own university course who share her hobbies and opinions. After a year, all new ideas sound the same. Which principle and which risk fit best?
o: Similarity, leading to an echo chamber
Exchange, leading to an echo chamber
Similarity, leading to many weak ties
soru.x: Ties built on a shared background and shared interests are the similarity principle, and its risk is an echo chamber where no new ideas come in. The “Exchange, echo chamber” option looks tempting because the risk is right, but exchange is a tie with people who are different; here everyone is alike.

adimlar.anlatim:
Ibarra advises managers to build three types of network. Each has a different purpose. The easiest way to separate them is to ask “which time does this network look at, and who does it serve?”

An Operational network is the people who help you do today’s job efficiently. The people who can block or support your project are in this network: a colleague in another department, the manager who gives approval, the supplier who provides materials. This network looks at today and serves the current work. Its members are largely set by the job; you do not choose them.

A Personal network is for your personal and professional development: referrals, outside information, coaching and mentoring. The examples in the course notes are alumni groups, clubs and professional associations. This network is usually outside the company and serves you and your career.

To keep the two apart, look at this: Is the person making contacts to finish today’s project, or to develop themselves and find support for their career? If it is the project, operational; if it is personal development, personal. The sentence “coaching and career advice from outside the company” always means personal.
adimlar.ornek: At an imaginary construction firm, the project manager Burcu meets regularly with the purchasing department and a city official to finish the building on time: operational network. In the evenings she goes to a professional association and gets coaching on her career from a retired engineer at another company: personal network.

soru.q: A junior architect meets monthly with a retired engineer from another firm who coaches her on her career, and she also joins a women-in-construction association. Which Ibarra network is she building?
soru.x: Coaching and mentoring from outside the company and a professional association are for personal development: personal network. Operational network looks tempting because the contacts are about work, but an operational network is made of people who help finish today’s project; the aim here is career development.

adimlar.anlatim:
The third type looks to the future. A Strategic network is the people who help you understand future priorities and challenges and win stakeholder support for them. This network may include industry experts, leaders from other fields, investors and community representatives. The aim is not to finish today’s work, but to see where to go tomorrow and to gather support behind you on the way there.

Put the three networks side by side on a timeline: operational aims at today, personal at your own development, and strategic at the future and the direction of the organization. The exam’s well-known distinction is this: outside people who give career advice are personal; people who help you see future trends and opportunities are strategic; colleagues you need for your current tasks are operational.

The course notes show that these principles can also work on a large scale with Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign: the campaign used social network principles. This example shows that network concepts are used not only for a personal career, but also to get a large organization moving.
adimlar.ornek: Selin, an imaginary hotel manager, meets regularly with city planners, tourism experts and local investors. Her aim is to understand how travel will change in five years and to gather support for the hotel’s green transition plan. These contacts do not help with today’s bookings; they show the future: strategic network.

soru.q: A hotel manager meets regularly with city planners, tourism experts and investors to understand where travel is heading over the next five years and to win their support for a new plan. Which Ibarra network is this?
soru.x: Understanding future trends and winning stakeholder support is the purpose of a strategic network. Personal network looks tempting because the contacts are outside the company, but a personal network is for a person’s own career development; the aim here is the future of the organization.

tuzaklar.yanlis: People outside the company who give coaching and career advice are a strategic network.
tuzaklar.dogru: Personal development, coaching and mentoring are a personal network. People who help you see future trends and opportunities are a strategic network.

tuzaklar.yanlis: The most valuable information always comes from your closest friends.
tuzaklar.dogru: According to Granovetter, people mostly find jobs through weak ties; distant contacts carry new information.

tuzaklar.yanlis: Reciprocity and exchange are the same principle; both are a trade of favours.
tuzaklar.dogru: Reciprocity is a return of equal value; exchange is trading complementary resources with people who are different.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A bridging tie is another name for a weak tie.
tuzaklar.dogru: Weak tie describes the strength of a tie; a bridging tie is a tie that carries non-redundant information you cannot get any other way.

tuzaklar.yanlis: A network built with similar people is the strongest and most innovative network.
tuzaklar.dogru: Similarity builds comfortable ties but carries the risk of an echo chamber: no new ideas come in.

ozet: Social network: a patterned set of relationships between actors; drawn in a sociogram.
Networks are the invisible organization: they show how communication and resources really flow.
Three advantages for leaders: access to information, access to diverse skills, power.
Strong ties mean frequent exchange, weak ties rare exchange; jobs are mostly found through weak ties.
A bridging tie carries information you cannot get any other way; centrality and density describe the shape of the network.
Kilduff and Tsai: reciprocity is equal return, exchange is complementary difference, similarity is shared background.
The risk of similarity is the echo chamber.
Ibarra: operational is today’s work, personal is your own development, strategic is the future and stakeholder support.
lessons.aklinda: Operational for today, personal for yourself, strategic for tomorrow.
lessons.sinavda: Part 2 describes a relationship someone builds or a trade of favours and asks which type of tie, which principle or which Ibarra network it is. It carries about 3 points. The difference between personal and strategic networks and the difference between reciprocity and exchange are the points that need the most care.
